engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening: Sicilian Defence Basics
chess.body: After 1.e4 c5 — Black fights for the centre asymmetrically. Black gets queenside counterplay; White gets kingside attack. Most common openings at club level. Learn one variation: Sicilian Najdorf (1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6). It's played by Kasparov, Fischer, Carlsen. Understand the plans before memorising moves.

wisdom.title: On Anger
wisdom.body: Anger is information, not instruction. It tells you a boundary was crossed or a value was violated. But acting on anger rarely solves the problem. Practice: when you feel it rising, say 'I need 5 minutes' and leave the room. Return calm. Then address the issue. You can be firm without being explosive.

book.author: Daniel Kahneman
book.chapter: System 1 vs System 2: Two Ways Your Brain Decides
book.lesson: Kahneman's central framework: System 1 is fast, automatic, emotional, unconscious — it drives 95% of decisions. System 2 is slow, deliberate, logical, effortful — it's what we think we use but rarely do. The problem: System 1 is riddled with biases and heuristics that made sense in evolutionary environments but lead to poor decisions in modern ones. Loss aversion (losses feel 2× more painful than equivalent gains feel good), anchoring (first number heard influences all subsequent judgements), availability bias (things that come to mind easily feel more probable) — all System 1 errors. Recognition is the first step to override.
book.key_quote: You are not as rational as you think. Your brain is a pattern-matching machine, not a logic processor.
book.action: Before your next important decision, write down your reasoning explicitly. Externalising it activates System 2 and reveals System 1 shortcuts.
crux: Two systems: System 1 is fast, automatic, emotional. System 2 is slow, effortful, logical.
System 2 is lazy and endorses System 1's answers with minimal checking.
What you see is all there is (WYSIATI). The mind builds confident stories from whatever is available.
Anchoring: an irrelevant number moves your estimate. Knowing this does not stop it.
Availability: vivid and recent events feel probable. Frequency gets confused with memorability.
Representativeness beats base rates. People pick the plausible story over the likelier category.
Loss aversion: losses hurt roughly 2x as much as equivalent gains please.
Prospect theory: you evaluate from a reference point, not in absolutes. Framing changes the answer.
Overconfidence is the most consequential bias, and expertise increases it.
The illusion of validity: confidence tracks story coherence, not predictive accuracy.
Regression to the mean explains most 'turnarounds' and most 'losses of form'.
The planning fallacy: forecasts default to best-case. Use the outside view and comparable past cases.
The remembering self and the experiencing self disagree. Memory is dominated by peaks and endings.
Formulas beat expert intuition in noisy, low-validity environments. Checklists and algorithms win.
learnings: You cannot debias yourself by intention. You can build procedures that catch the bias.
Fluency masquerades as truth. Anything easy to process feels more likely.
Expert intuition is real only where feedback is fast and regular. Markets do not qualify.
Write the forecast down before the outcome, or hindsight will rewrite it.
examples: Israeli parole judges granted parole ~65% of the time right after a meal break and near 0% just before one. Same evidence, different glucose.
The Linda problem: most people rate 'bank teller and feminist' as likelier than 'bank teller', which is logically impossible.
Kahneman's flight-instructor insight: praise after a good flight seemed to hurt and criticism after a bad one seemed to help. It was regression to the mean, not feedback working.
adapt: Write the trade thesis before entry. Post-hoc explanation is System 1 inventing a story.
Use base rates on the Dubai search: what fraction of applications convert? Plan on that, not on the best case.
The planning fallacy is why estimates slip. Take the outside view — how long did the last comparable build actually take?
Backtest numbers over gut feel. -0.029R on 1H means the 1H feeling is wrong, however strong it is.

minimalism.title: Owning Is A Liability
minimalism.body: Every object requires storage, maintenance, insurance, cleaning, moving, and eventual disposal. The purchase price is the smallest number in that list. Accountants of all people should price the full cost.
minimalism.action: Before the next purchase, write the 5-year total cost of ownership.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Handle The Bill Without Theatre
etiquette.body: Decide before you arrive. Settle it quietly. The public wrestle over a bill embarrasses everyone at the table.
etiquette.action: Settle the next bill before it reaches the table.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Keep A Line A Day
stillness.body: One sentence about the day. Not a journal habit that collapses in a week — one line. In ten years it becomes the only accurate record of your life that exists.
stillness.action: Write one line tonight. Date it.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Base Rates
model.body: Before believing your case is special, ask what usually happens. Most restaurants fail. Most projects overrun. Most traders lose. Your plan starts from that number, not from zero.
model.action: Find the base rate for your current bet before adjusting for your edge.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: Getting attention politely — a waiter, a stranger, someone in your way.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: The Five Whys
drill.body: Ask why five times to get from symptom to cause. Most analysis stops at why one and fixes a symptom, which guarantees the problem returns.
drill.action: Take one recurring problem. Ask why five times. Write each answer.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Light Sets The Clock
health.body: Morning daylight within an hour of waking anchors circadian rhythm and improves sleep that night more reliably than any supplement. Outdoor light is 10–100x brighter than indoor, even when overcast.
health.action: Ten minutes outside within an hour of waking. No sunglasses.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Marc Benioff
quote.quote: The secret to successful hiring is this: look for the people who want to change the world.

lesson.lesson: Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without.

case.title: Netflix: DVD to Streaming (2007)
case.story: Netflix had a profitable DVD business. Reed Hastings cannibalized it by betting on streaming. Blockbuster laughed. Netflix is now worth $250B+.
case.lesson: Disrupt yourself before someone else does. The most dangerous competitor is your own comfort.

fpna.title: Rolling Forecast
fpna.body: Rolling 12-month forecasts beat static annual budgets. Less time defending, more time deciding.

cfo.title: CFO Interview: Top 5 Questions
cfo.body: 1. What's your capital allocation philosophy? 2. How do you manage a cash crisis? 3. Describe a time you stopped a bad investment. 4. How do you build trust with the CEO? 5. Walk me through a fundraise or M&A you led. Practice until smooth.

money_hack.title: Expense Tracking
money_hack.body: Track every expense for 30 days. You will find ₹3–5K of invisible leaks.

dubai.title: Your CV is being read by software
dubai.body: Most Gulf groups run Taleo or SuccessFactors. Two columns, tables, headers and a photo all parse to garbage. Single column, standard headings, .docx not PDF, no logos.
dubai.targets: Job title in the CV header must match the job title in the posting. Literally.
dubai.action: Rewrite the top third of the CV as: title, then five bullets, each with a number in it.

desk.productivity: End every meeting with: who does what by when. No action = no meeting.

father.title: Offer food she can hold
father.do: Soft strips she can grip herself — steamed carrot, banana, well-cooked pasta. Accept the mess.
father.why: Self-feeding at 7 months develops the pincer grip and, more importantly, lets her control intake. Children who regulate their own portions early are less likely to over-eat later.

father.title: Protect the sleep routine
father.do: Same order, same lighting, same time — bath, feed, book, bed. Do it yourself at least twice a week.
father.why: Consistency of sequence matters more than the exact timing. Fathers who own bedtime regularly build a distinct attachment relationship rather than a substitute one.

life_wisdom.teaching: Seeing things as they are, before preference distorts them. The first of the three jewels, and deliberately placed before right conduct.
life_wisdom.apply: Separate the number from what you want the number to be. Write the actual result before writing the explanation — the order changes the explanation.

life_wisdom.teaching: The Buddha's image: struck by an arrow, most people fire a second one into themselves — the story about what the first arrow means.
life_wisdom.apply: A stopped-out trade is the first arrow. 'I am bad at this' is the second. Only one of them was caused by the market.

vocab.meaning: To make a bad situation better.
vocab.example: The payment plan ameliorated the cash position without fixing it.
vocab.note: Implies improvement without resolution — which is often the honest description.

vocab.example: Notwithstanding the shortfall, cash generation held.
vocab.note: Can lead the sentence or follow the noun. A single well-placed use signals command of register.

speaking.title: End the sentence
speaking.drill: Read three sentences aloud and drop your pitch on the final word of each. Record and check you are not rising at the end.
speaking.why: Upward inflection turns statements into questions. It is the fastest way to sound unsure of numbers you are certain about.

interview_tech.q: Explain deferred tax to a board member in 60 seconds.
interview_tech.a: Accounting profit and taxable profit are computed under different rules, so tax paid this year rarely matches tax on this year's reported profit. Deferred tax records the future consequence of that gap. The classic retail example is accelerated capital allowances on fit-out: you get the tax relief early, so you owe more tax later — that future obligation sits as a deferred tax liability. It is not cash and it is not a provision for a dispute; it is timing. Say that last sentence, because it is what they are actually worried about.

interview_tech.q: How do you measure promotional effectiveness properly?
interview_tech.a: Incremental margin, not uplift. Take the sales during the promotion, subtract what the baseline would have been without it, subtract the margin given away on units that would have sold at full price anyway, and subtract any cannibalisation of adjacent full-price lines. The result is often negative for deep discounts on already-popular SKUs. Use a control group of comparable stores where operationally possible — without a counterfactual, every promotion looks successful because sales always rise.

interview_soft.q: What would your last manager say is your weakness?
interview_soft.a: Name a real one with a boundary. The pattern that works: a genuine weakness, evidence you know its cost, and the specific mechanism you use to contain it. 'I go too deep into detail before surfacing a view — it has cost me time on low-stakes analysis. I now set a decision deadline before starting and present at that point regardless of how complete it feels.' Avoid perfectionism, avoid anything that would disqualify you for the role itself.

interview_soft.q: What is the hardest decision you have made in your career?
interview_soft.a: Hard means genuinely two-sided, not merely unpleasant. Redundancies, closing a site, overruling someone you respected, or choosing between two people for one role. Structure: the trade-off, the information you had and did not have, how you decided, what it cost, and what you would do differently. Interviewers discount any answer where the right choice was obvious in hindsight — say what made it genuinely close.
